sections.text:
The Secret of Roman Concrete

A. Along the coasts of the Mediterranean, the remains of Roman harbours still stand in the waves, their piers battered by salt water for some two thousand years. In Rome itself, the Pantheon, completed in the second century AD, still carries the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Such survivals are all the more striking when set beside the record of modern construction. Many of the bridges, car parks and sea walls built during the twentieth century began to crack and crumble within fifty or a hundred years, and engineers today typically design new structures to last around a century. The contrast has prompted a simple but persistent question: what did Roman builders understand that their modern successors have overlooked?

B. Part of the answer lies in the ingredients. Modern concrete is held together by Portland cement, a material patented in Britain in the early nineteenth century and made by heating limestone and clay in kilns to about 1,450°C. Roman builders instead combined lime with volcanic ash, the best of which was dug from deposits around the Bay of Naples, near the town of Pozzuoli. Their lime was produced at roughly 900°C, a far lower temperature, and the ash supplied silica and alumina that reacted with it to form a dense, stone-like binder. Into this paste workers packed fist-sized chunks of rock or broken brick, building up walls and foundations layer by layer rather than pouring a liquid mixture into moulds, as is common practice today.

C. For centuries, observers assumed that the harbour structures had simply been lucky, or that the calm waters of the Mediterranean had treated them unusually kindly. Seawater normally attacks concrete: salts seep into tiny pores and react with the cement, causing it to swell and split. Yet when a team led by the geologist Ines Varga examined cores drilled from an ancient pier, they found the opposite process at work. As seawater percolated through the material, it dissolved some of the volcanic ash and allowed new minerals to grow in the spaces left behind. Long, plate-shaped crystals had formed within the pores and cracks, interlocking like the fibres of a woven mat. Rather than weakening the concrete, the sea appeared to have been slowly reinforcing it, so that the oldest sections were in some respects stronger than when they were first built.

D. A second clue came from something earlier researchers had dismissed as a flaw. Roman concrete is dotted with small white lumps of lime, a few millimetres across, which were long blamed on careless mixing or poor-quality materials. Materials scientist Tomas Reyes and his colleagues argued instead that these lumps, known as lime clasts, were a by-product of 'hot mixing', in which builders added quicklime directly to the ash and water, generating intense heat. To test the idea, the team made samples using this method, deliberately cracked them and then allowed water to run through the gaps. Within two weeks the cracks had sealed completely: the water had dissolved calcium from the clasts, which then recrystallised as calcium carbonate and filled the openings. Identical samples made without the clasts continued to leak.

E. None of this means that Roman concrete is simply superior. It is considerably weaker under compression than its modern equivalent, and it hardens slowly, sometimes over months, whereas contractors today expect a new floor slab to bear loads within days. Nor could it support the slender towers and long spans of contemporary architecture. These depend on steel bars embedded in the concrete to resist bending and stretching, and here lies a paradox. Steel gives modern structures much of their strength, but once moisture and salt reach it, the metal begins to rust. Because rust occupies more space than the original steel, it pushes outwards and breaks the surrounding concrete apart from within. Roman builders, who used no such reinforcement, never faced this particular form of decay.

F. Engineers are now trying to combine the strengths of both traditions. Few expect ancient recipes simply to replace modern ones. Cement production is responsible for roughly eight per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions, partly because of the fuel burned to reach such high kiln temperatures, so a mixture that needs less heat and lasts longer could bring considerable environmental benefits. Several laboratories are experimenting with recipes that add volcanic ash, or industrial waste with similar chemistry, to modern cement, and some are testing whether lime clasts could give new buildings the ability to repair their own cracks. The coastal engineer Marta Lindqvist believes Roman-style concrete may prove most valuable for sea walls and other marine structures, where corrosion is the greatest threat. She warns, however, that promising laboratory results do not guarantee success outdoors. 'The Romans had centuries to demonstrate that their concrete worked,' she says. 'We will need patience before we can claim the same for ours.'

sections.text:
Archives in the Ice

A. Every winter, snow falls on the high plateaus of Greenland and Antarctica, and in the coldest parts of those ice sheets it never melts. Instead, each year's snow is buried by the next, and over centuries the weight above squeezes the fluffy crystals into dense glacial ice. As this happens, small pockets of the atmosphere become sealed between the grains. The result is a frozen archive, stacked in order from the most recent snowfall at the surface to the oldest ice near the rock beneath, and reading it has become one of the most powerful ways of discovering what the Earth's climate was like long before anyone kept weather records.

B. Retrieving the archive begins with choosing where to drill. According to glaciologist Mirela Kossak, who has led several expeditions for the Polar Stratigraphy Group, the ideal site is a broad dome where the ice is thick but moves slowly. "Near the coast, ice flows towards the sea and its layers get stretched and tangled," she explains. "On a dome, they stay roughly where they were laid down." The drill itself is a hollow rotating tube with cutting teeth at its lower end. Lowered on a cable, it carves out a cylinder of ice a few metres long, which is hauled to the surface before the drill descends again. Because the enormous pressure at depth would gradually squeeze the borehole shut, the hole is filled with a fluid whose density roughly matches that of the surrounding ice. Reaching the bottom of a sheet three kilometres thick can take several summer seasons.

C. Not every core can travel straight away. At depths of a few hundred metres, the trapped air is under such high pressure that the ice tends to crack or shatter when it is brought up. Kossak's team found that this brittle ice could be handled safely only if it was left to rest in a cold store at the drilling site for about a year, allowing the stresses inside it to relax. Eventually, each section is measured, photographed and labelled with its depth before being packed into insulated containers and shipped to a laboratory, where it is kept well below freezing, since even brief warming could alter its chemistry.

D. Before any measurement means anything, the ice has to be dated. In the upper part of a core, this can be done by counting annual layers, much as one might count the rings of a tree. Summer and winter snow differ in texture and in the amount of dust and sea salt they contain, so each year usually leaves a recognisable band. Deeper down, however, the weight above has thinned the layers until they are too narrow to tell apart. Here researchers turn to other clues. Thin bands of ash from large volcanic eruptions act as time markers that can be matched between cores and sometimes linked to eruptions of known date. Beyond that, computer models of how the ice has flowed and compressed are used to estimate the ages of the deepest sections.

E. With a timescale in place, the analysis can begin. The most widely used temperature signal comes from the water itself. Oxygen atoms exist in lighter and heavier forms, and the colder the air when snow forms, the smaller the proportion of heavy oxygen it contains. By measuring this ratio along a core, scientists can trace past warming and cooling. The bubbles offer something more direct: genuine samples of ancient atmosphere, in which concentrations of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane can be measured. Dust provides a third line of evidence, since ice laid down during glacial periods typically contains far more of it, reflecting a drier, windier world.

F. Impressive as these records are, they have limits. One problem is that the air in a bubble is always younger than the ice around it. Near the surface, snow remains porous for decades or longer, and air keeps circulating through it until the pores finally close. At sites with very little snowfall, the gap between the age of the ice and that of its air can reach several thousand years, and it must be estimated rather than measured. The bottom of the sheet brings further difficulty: heat rising from the rock can melt the deepest ice, and layers close to the bed are often folded, so the oldest part of the record may be scrambled or missing. Finally, a core describes conditions at a single location. Kossak warns that a temperature history from central Antarctica should not be treated as a global average, and that ice records are most valuable when compared with evidence from ocean sediments and caves.

G. At present, the longest continuous ice-core record reaches back about 800,000 years. Many researchers hope to go further, to a period roughly a million years ago when the rhythm of the ice ages appears to have changed. Ice that old will only be found where the bed is cold and the ice has barely moved, and the Polar Stratigraphy Group has spent three seasons surveying possible sites with radar. Kossak is cautiously optimistic: such ice probably exists, she says, but it may form a layer only a few metres thick at the very bottom of the sheet.

questions.prompt: According to Kossak, in which part of an ice sheet do the layers become stretched and tangled?
questions.evidence: Near the coast, ice flows towards the sea and its layers get stretched and tangled

explanation.ru: В абзаце B приводятся слова Коссак о том, что у побережья лёд течёт к морю, из-за чего его слои растягиваются и перепутываются. Поэтому она предпочитает купол вдали от побережья.
explanation.uk: В абзаці B наведено слова Коссак про те, що біля узбережжя лід тече до моря, через що його шари розтягуються й переплутуються. Тому вона віддає перевагу куполу далеко від узбережжя.

questions.evidence: Reaching the bottom of a sheet three kilometres thick can take several summer seasons.

explanation.ru: В абзаце B сказано, что, чтобы добраться до дна ледяного щита толщиной три километра, может понадобиться несколько летних сезонов. Выражение «ice three kilometres deep» в вопросе — это перефразировка «a sheet three kilometres thick».
explanation.uk: В абзаці B сказано, що, щоб дістатися дна крижаного щита завтовшки три кілометри, може знадобитися кілька літніх сезонів. Вираз «ice three kilometres deep» у питанні — це перефразування «a sheet three kilometres thick».

questions.prompt: Apart from carbon dioxide, which greenhouse gas does the passage say can be measured in the trapped bubbles?

explanation.en: Paragraph E explains that the bubbles are real samples of old air, and names carbon dioxide and methane as gases measured in them.
explanation.ru: В абзаце E объясняется, что пузырьки — это настоящие образцы древнего воздуха, а среди газов, которые в них измеряют, названы углекислый газ («carbon dioxide») и метан («methane»).

questions.evidence: ice laid down during glacial periods typically contains far more of it, reflecting a drier, windier world

explanation.ru: В абзаце E говорится, что лёд ледниковых периодов обычно содержит гораздо больше пыли («dust»). Это говорит о том, что мир тогда был суше и ветренее.
explanation.uk: В абзаці E сказано, що лід льодовикових періодів зазвичай містить набагато більше пилу («dust»). Це свідчить про те, що світ тоді був сухішим і вітрянішим.

explanation.uk: В абзаці C сказано, що кожен фрагмент маркують («labelled»), а потім пакують у теплоізольовані контейнери («insulated containers») для відправлення до лабораторії.

Researchers want to study a time when the pattern of ice ages seems to have shifted.
Kossak doubts that such ancient ice exists.
Suitable ice is likely to be found only where the ground beneath it is cold.
The group has already recovered ice that is over a million years old.

questions.prompt: Which TWO of the following statements about the search for older ice are supported by the passage?
questions.evidence: a period roughly a million years ago when the rhythm of the ice ages appears to have changed. Ice that old will only be found where the bed is cold

explanation.en: Paragraph G says researchers want to reach a time when the rhythm of the ice ages seems to have changed, and that such ice will only be found where the bed is cold. The longest record so far is about 800,000 years, and Kossak thinks the ice probably exists but may be only a few metres thick, so E, A and C are wrong.
explanation.ru: В абзаце G сказано, что исследователи хотят добраться до времени, когда ритм ледниковых периодов, по-видимому, изменился, и что такой лёд можно найти только там, где ложе холодное. Самая длинная запись на сегодня охватывает около 800 000 лет, а Коссак считает, что такой лёд, вероятно, существует, но может быть толщиной всего несколько метров, поэтому варианты «E», «A» и «C» неверны.
explanation.uk: В абзаці G сказано, що дослідники хочуть дістатися часу, коли ритм льодовикових періодів, схоже, змінився, і що такий лід можна знайти лише там, де ложе холодне. Найдовший запис на сьогодні охоплює близько 800 000 років, а Коссак вважає, що такий лід, імовірно, існує, але може мати товщину лише кілька метрів, тому варіанти «E», «A» і «C» неправильні.

groups.instruction: Choose TWO letters, A–E, for each question.

sections.text:
In Defence of Boredom

A. Few states of mind have a worse reputation than boredom. We speak of being "bored to death", we apologise to guests if an evening drags, and we treat a dull afternoon as time that has simply been lost. Modern life has organised itself around making sure that such afternoons never happen: an entire entertainment industry now competes to fill every spare minute, and the smartphone means that nobody need endure even a few seconds of empty time in a queue or on a station platform. The assumption behind all this is that boredom is a defect, something to be cured as quickly as possible. I believe this assumption is wrong. A moderate amount of boredom is not merely bearable; it is one of the more useful experiences an ordinary day can offer.

B. To see why, it helps to consider what boredom actually is. Psychologists generally describe it as an uncomfortable state in which we have attention to spare but can find nothing that seems worth spending it on. Understood in this way, boredom is less like an illness and more like hunger. Hunger is unpleasant, yet nobody regards it as a fault in the body; it is a message that we need to eat. Boredom, similarly, tells us that what we are currently doing is not rewarding enough and that we should change it. It is a signal, not a malfunction. Reaching for a distraction the moment it appears is rather like swallowing a painkiller to cope with a stone in your shoe: the discomfort fades, but the cause remains exactly where it was.

C. The habit of silencing this signal may also be changing our attention itself. The attention researcher Marta Lindqvist followed two groups of commuters for six weeks. One group used their phones throughout every journey; the other agreed to travel without them. At the end of the period, both groups were given the same unexciting reading task, and those who had spent their journeys on their phones rated it as more tedious and abandoned it considerably earlier. Lindqvist's interpretation is that constant stimulation raises the threshold at which ordinary tasks begin to feel tedious, so that activities which once seemed acceptable come to feel intolerable. Her study was small, and I would not claim that it proves phones damage concentration on their own; people who choose to look at screens all day may differ in other ways. But it fits an experience many of us will recognise: the more entertainment we consume, the less patience we seem to have for anything that is not entertaining.

D. Boredom's best-known defenders point to creativity, and here there is genuine evidence, though less than enthusiasts suggest. In one experiment by the cognitive psychologist Tomas Ferreira, volunteers spent twenty minutes sorting a large box of buttons by colour, while a second group watched a short comedy clip. Both groups were then given the opening of a story and asked to write as many different endings as they could. The button-sorters produced a noticeably wider range of endings. Ferreira believes that when the outside world offers too little, the mind begins to wander in search of the stimulation it lacks, and this wandering brings unrelated ideas together. It is an attractive finding, but popular writing has often turned it into a promise that boredom will make anyone inventive. It will not. Boredom creates room for new ideas; it does not supply them.

E. Nor should every kind of boredom be welcomed. Chronic boredom, the kind experienced by people confined for long periods or trapped in work of unbroken monotony, is associated with low mood, poor health and risky behaviour. I have no wish to defend it. The distinction that matters is between a passing episode, which we are free to respond to, and a lasting condition from which there is no way out. The value of brief boredom lies precisely in that response: it pushes us to look for something better to do, to think, or to notice what is around us. When escape is impossible, the signal becomes nothing more than suffering.

F. This is why I think the modern instinct to rescue children from boredom deserves more scrutiny. Many parents feel that a child complaining of having nothing to do represents a failure on their part, and they hurry to provide an activity or a screen. Yet children who are left to deal with empty time themselves often learn to invent their own occupations, constructing games, stories and projects that no adult would have thought to suggest. In removing the discomfort, we may also remove the opportunity to discover how to make use of it.

G. None of this means that we should seek out tedium or abandon entertainment. The practical lesson is modest. Leave the phone in your pocket during short waits; let a slow train journey be slow; notice the restless feeling of boredom and ask what it is telling you before deciding what to do about it. The goal is not to enjoy being bored, but to stop running from it, and to treat it as information rather than as an enemy.
sections.title: In Defence of Boredom

questions.prompt: The widespread belief that boredom should be eliminated as quickly as possible is mistaken.
questions.evidence: I believe this assumption is wrong.

explanation.en: In paragraph A the writer describes the common assumption that boredom is a defect to be cured, and then says directly that this assumption is wrong.
explanation.ru: В абзаце A автор описывает распространённое представление о том, что скука — это недостаток, который нужно лечить, а затем прямо говорит, что это представление ошибочно.
explanation.uk: В абзаці A автор описує поширене уявлення про те, що нудьга — це вада, яку треба лікувати, а потім прямо каже, що це уявлення хибне.

questions.prompt: Feeling bored shows that the mind is not working properly.
questions.evidence: It is a signal, not a malfunction.

explanation.en: In paragraph B the writer says boredom is a useful message, like hunger, and specifically not a malfunction. The statement says the opposite.
explanation.ru: В абзаце B автор пишет, что скука — полезный сигнал, как голод, и подчёркивает, что это вовсе не сбой. В утверждении сказано обратное.
explanation.uk: В абзаці B автор пише, що нудьга — корисний сигнал, як голод, і наголошує, що це зовсім не збій. Твердження каже протилежне.

questions.prompt: Lindqvist's study demonstrates that phones by themselves reduce people's ability to concentrate.
questions.evidence: I would not claim that it proves phones damage concentration on their own

explanation.en: In paragraph C the writer says the study was small and does not prove that phones alone harm concentration, because phone users may differ in other ways.
explanation.ru: В абзаце C автор отмечает, что исследование было небольшим и не доказывает, что концентрацию ухудшают именно телефоны сами по себе: пользователи телефонов могут отличаться и по другим признакам.
explanation.uk: В абзаці C автор зазначає, що дослідження було невеликим і не доводить, що концентрацію погіршують саме телефони самі по собі, адже користувачі телефонів можуть відрізнятися й за іншими ознаками.

questions.prompt: The connection between boredom and creativity has been exaggerated in popular writing.
questions.evidence: popular writing has often turned it into a promise that boredom will make anyone inventive. It will not.

explanation.en: In paragraph D the writer accepts there is some evidence but says popular writing promises too much, since boredom does not make everyone inventive.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D автор признаёт, что определённые данные есть, но считает, что популярные тексты обещают слишком много: скука делает изобретательным далеко не каждого.
explanation.uk: В абзаці D автор визнає, що певні докази є, але вважає, що популярні тексти обіцяють забагато: нудьга робить винахідливим далеко не кожного.

questions.prompt: Schools should give pupils more unstructured time during the day.

explanation.en: Paragraph F discusses parents rescuing children from boredom at home, but the writer never mentions schools or timetables, so their view on this is unknown.
explanation.ru: В абзаце F речь идёт о родителях, которые дома спасают детей от скуки, но о школах и расписании автор нигде не упоминает, поэтому его мнение на этот счёт неизвестно.
explanation.uk: В абзаці F ідеться про батьків, які вдома рятують дітей від нудьги, але про школи й розклад автор ніде не згадує, тож його думка щодо цього невідома.

groups.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in the passage? Write YES if the statement agrees with the views of the writer, NO if the statement contradicts the views of the writer, or NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this.

options.text: frequently create activities that adults would not have suggested.
came up with a greater variety of story endings.
leaves people with no means of escape.
rated the reading task as less tedious than the other group did.
has mental capacity available but no worthwhile use for it.
indicates that a change of activity is needed.
gave up a dull reading task earlier than the other group.
wrote fewer endings than people who had watched a comedy clip.
is usually a sign of physical illness.

questions.prompt: Psychologists see boredom as a state in which a person
questions.evidence: an uncomfortable state in which we have attention to spare but can find nothing that seems worth spending it on

explanation.en: Paragraph B: having attention to spare is restated as having mental capacity available, and finding nothing worth spending it on as having no worthwhile use for it.
explanation.ru: Абзац B: мысль о том, что у человека есть свободное внимание, передана как наличие незанятых умственных ресурсов, а то, что его не на что стоящее потратить, — как отсутствие для них достойного применения.
explanation.uk: Абзац B: думку про те, що людина має вільну увагу, передано як наявність незайнятих розумових ресурсів, а те, що її немає на що варте витратити, — як відсутність для них гідного застосування.

questions.prompt: Like hunger, boredom
questions.evidence: Boredom, similarly, tells us that what we are currently doing is not rewarding enough and that we should change it

explanation.en: Paragraph B compares boredom with hunger: both are messages, and boredom tells us to change what we are doing. Ending I is wrong because the writer says boredom is less like an illness.
explanation.ru: В абзаце B скука сравнивается с голодом: и то и другое — сигналы, и скука подсказывает нам, что пора сменить занятие. Вариант I не подходит, потому что, по словам автора, скука как раз меньше похожа на болезнь.
explanation.uk: В абзаці B нудьгу порівнюють із голодом: і те, і інше — сигнали, і нудьга підказує нам, що час змінити заняття. Варіант I не підходить, бо, за словами автора, нудьга якраз менше схожа на хворобу.

questions.prompt: Commuters who used their phones throughout their journeys
questions.evidence: those who had spent their journeys on their phones rated it as more tedious and abandoned it considerably earlier

explanation.en: Paragraph C says the phone users abandoned the reading task earlier. Ending D is wrong because they found the task more tedious, not less.
explanation.ru: В абзаце C сказано, что пользователи телефонов раньше бросали задание на чтение. Вариант D неверен: задание показалось им более скучным, а не менее.
explanation.uk: В абзаці C сказано, що користувачі телефонів раніше кидали завдання з читання. Варіант D неправильний: завдання здалося їм нуднішим, а не менш нудним.

questions.prompt: Volunteers who had spent twenty minutes sorting buttons
questions.evidence: The button-sorters produced a noticeably wider range of endings.

explanation.en: Paragraph D says the button-sorters produced a wider range of story endings. Ending H reverses the result.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D сказано, что участники, сортировавшие пуговицы, придумали более разнообразные концовки историй. Вариант H переворачивает этот результат.
explanation.uk: В абзаці D сказано, що учасники, які сортували ґудзики, вигадали різноманітніші кінцівки історій. Варіант H перевертає цей результат.

questions.prompt: Chronic boredom, unlike brief boredom,
questions.evidence: a lasting condition from which there is no way out

explanation.en: Paragraph E contrasts a passing episode that we can respond to with a lasting condition from which there is no way out.
explanation.ru: В абзаце E противопоставляются временный эпизод, на который можно как-то отреагировать, и устойчивое состояние, из которого нет выхода.
explanation.uk: В абзаці E протиставлено тимчасовий епізод, на який можна якось відреагувати, і стійкий стан, з якого немає виходу.

groups.instruction: Complete each sentence with the correct ending, A–I, from the box below. Write the correct letter, A–I. You may use each letter only once.

questions.prompt: According to the writer, a whole ______ now tries to occupy people's every free moment.
questions.evidence: an entire entertainment industry now competes to fill every spare minute

explanation.en: Paragraph A says an entire entertainment industry competes to fill every spare minute; 'every free moment' restates 'every spare minute'.
explanation.ru: В абзаце A говорится, что целая индустрия развлечений соперничает за то, чтобы заполнить каждую свободную минуту; «every free moment» — это перефразировка «every spare minute».
explanation.uk: В абзаці A сказано, що ціла індустрія розваг змагається за те, щоб заповнити кожну вільну хвилину; «every free moment» — це перефразування «every spare minute».

questions.prompt: The writer compares escaping boredom through distraction to taking medicine for the pain caused by a ______ in your shoe.
questions.evidence: swallowing a painkiller to cope with a stone in your shoe

explanation.en: Paragraph B: reaching for a distraction is like swallowing a painkiller for a stone in your shoe, because the cause of the discomfort stays.
explanation.ru: Абзац B: хвататься за развлечение — всё равно что глотать обезболивающее, когда в ботинок попал камешек: причина дискомфорта никуда не девается.
explanation.uk: Абзац B: хапатися за розвагу — те саме, що ковтати знеболювальне, коли в черевик потрапив камінчик: причина дискомфорту нікуди не зникає.

questions.prompt: Lindqvist argues that constant stimulation increases the ______ at which everyday tasks start to seem dull.
questions.evidence: constant stimulation raises the threshold at which ordinary tasks begin to feel tedious

explanation.en: Paragraph C gives Lindqvist's interpretation: stimulation 'raises the threshold' at which ordinary tasks feel tedious.
explanation.ru: В абзаце C приводится толкование Линдквиста: стимуляция «raises the threshold», то есть повышает порог, за которым обычные дела начинают казаться скучными.
explanation.uk: В абзаці C наведено тлумачення Ліндквіста: стимуляція «raises the threshold», тобто підвищує поріг, за яким звичайні справи починають здаватися нудними.

questions.prompt: Ferreira thinks that a mind given too little by the outside world will start to ______ while it looks for stimulation.
questions.evidence: the mind begins to wander in search of the stimulation it lacks

explanation.en: Paragraph D: when the outside world offers too little, the mind begins to wander in search of stimulation.
explanation.ru: Абзац D: когда внешний мир даёт слишком мало, ум начинает блуждать в поисках стимуляции.
explanation.uk: Абзац D: коли зовнішній світ дає занадто мало, розум починає блукати в пошуках стимуляції.
